cards.body:
Mercy Perry's car will not start after Saturday's flooding in Indiantown brought water up to his front door. Perry said the village used to have fairly good drainage and never had flooding like this before. On Monday, as more rain fell in Indiantown, residents looked at the sky with worry.

Village manager Taryn Kryzda said 6 inches of rain on Saturday simply overwhelmed the drainage system, causing the flooding. She said the village found even in new development that the drainage structures were compromised because of so much rain in a short period of time. Perry said he did see village crews out clearing debris from drains on Saturday.

Upgrading the drainage infrastructure would take time and money, according to Kryzda. She said the village must first do the engineering, and has already engaged engineers to start that process. Then the village will create a capital improvement program to prioritize projects and identify funding.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill. The credits result from the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro, the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, will receive an estimated $64 credit.

In June, the City Council voted to return all of the settlement money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience.

The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Council members agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Councilman Anthony Bonna said it's the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

hero.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use for a data center. The rezoning application states the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned light industrial.

 The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center because of existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system.

 The rezoning application requests the remaining 26 acres be zoned general commercial for development of commercial retail uses, which could include a hotel, gas station, restaurants, or fast food establishments. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption, and no noise pollution. Broderick said if they don't demonstrate these protections, he will not be supportive of the proposal.

According to the rezoning application, if approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. The partner company would need to submit a site plan application to the city and obtain approval of the site plan.

Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area. When asked about the potential data center, she said she hates the idea. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions. Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption, and no noise pollution.

Broderick said data centers are kind of the rage right now, but added that if developers do not meet his conditions, he will not be supportive of the project. The rezoning application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September.

cards.body:
Willow Lakes LLC submitted a rezoning application in June to St. Lucie County to change 174 acres of its 203-acre property off West Midway Road and Interstate 95 to light industrial use for a data center. The rezoning application states the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned light industrial.

 The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center because of existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system.

 The rezoning application requests the remaining 26 acres be zoned general commercial for development of commercial retail uses, which could include a hotel, gas station, restaurants, or fast food establishments. Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption, and no noise pollution. Broderick said if they don't demonstrate these protections, he will not be supportive of the proposal.

 Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area. When asked about the potential data center, Whiteside said she hates the idea. The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board in September. If rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center and submit a site plan application to the city for approval.

The settlement resolved the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. "Because it makes it better. You have maggots crawling out of the trash. I'd rather go back to twice a week," Koon-Martin said.
